stories.summary: African Development Bank Group and Agence FranÃ§aise De DÃ©veloppement Renew Partnership to Accelerate Joint Investments Across Africa 12 November 2026 Content from a Premium Partner African Development Bank (Abidjan) The African Development Bank Group and Agence Française de Développement (AFD) have signed a memorandum of understanding for 2026-2031, building on a partnership that has supported 17 jointly financed projects across 14 African countries since 2021. Signed on 10 November, on the sidelines of the Paris Peace Forum, the agreement aims to strengthen cooperation from the earliest stages of project development and maintain close alignment through implementation. By jointly assessing prospective projects as early as possible and combining financing with project preparation, technical advice, policy dialogue and capacity building, the two institutions aim to build a stronger pipeline of investment-ready projects and programmes. They also intend to deepen collaboration on project management, monitoring and knowledge transfer. Priority areas include infrastructure for the energy transition, transport, water and sanitation, and regional connectivity, as well as agriculture and industry.

stories.title: Niger: UNHRC Calls For Millions in Emergency Aid to Fill Critical Gaps
stories.summary: Niger: UNHRC Calls For Millions in Emergency Aid to Fill Critical Gaps Anna Jefferys/IRIN Refugees who have fled Boko Haram violence (file photo). 12 November 2026 allAfrica.com By Peter Kenny Geneva — The UN Refugee Agency, UNHCR, warned on Tuesday of a deepening crisis that has caused tens of thousands of people to flee from Nigeria to neighbouring Niger and Benin, where problems of malnutrition and disease are surfacing. Dominique Hyde, UNHCR director of external relations, said at a UN press conference in Geneva that nearly 64,000 people have arrived in Niger fleeing violence in northern Nigeria since the beginning of the year. “They are adding to the growing humanitarian needs in a country already hosting more than half a million refugees and asylum-seekers, including some 327,500 from Nigeria, alongside people displaced within Niger itself,” said Hyde. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn In the past decade, attacks by Boko Haram, Islamic State West Africa Province (ISWAP) fighters and criminal gangs have displaced millions of people fleeing the violence. “The impact of the violence is also being felt further afield, with several hundred Nigerians seeking refuge in neighbouring Benin,” said Hyde. “Although the numbers remain relatively small compared to arrivals in Niger, these movements highlight the widening geographical impact of insecurity in northern Nigeria and the increasing distances families are travelling in search of safety.” UNHCR said that most arrivals have sought safety in Diffa, in south-eastern Niger, and Tahoua, in western Niger, both bordering Nigeria, which are already grappling with insecurity, climate shocks and overstretched services. The refugee agency said in October alone, around 1,200 people crossed into Diffa and another 3,400 into Tahoua, as violence continued to force families from their homes. THOUSANDS OF NEWLY-ARRIVED REFUGEES “Thousands of newly arrived refugees, many of them children, are struggling to survive with limited access to food, clean water, shelter and essential services, as humanitarian resources fall critically short,” noted Hyde.

stories.summary: Nigerian Court Detains Journalist Daniel Ojukwu On Cybercrime Charges Ye Jinghan / Unsplash (File photo) 11 November 2026 Committee to Protect Journalists (New York) Abuja — The Committee to Protect Journalists calls on Nigerian authorities to immediately drop the criminal charges against journalist Daniel Ojukwu, release him unconditionally, and stop criminalizing the press for their work. On November 10, a federal court in Nigeria's capital, Abuja, remanded Ojukwu, a correspondent with the privately owned Foundation for Investigative Journalism (FIJ), to the Kuje Custodial Centre until December 1 on cybercrime and criminal defamation charges, according to a copy of the charge sheet, which CPJ reviewed. Ojukwu, who traveled to the hearing from the southwestern Lagos state, pleaded not guilty to the 12 counts brought against him. FIJ's founder and award-winning journalist, Fisayo Soyombo, who faces the same charges, was not in court but is expected at the next hearing, according to FIJ's lawyers, Oluseye Ayo Moore and Abimbola Ojenike, who spoke with CPJ. "Nigerian authorities must swiftly drop the criminal charges against journalist Daniel Ojukwu and FIJ founder Fisayo Soyombo, and repeal laws that criminalize journalism," said CPJ Africa Director Angela Quintal. "Nigeria's cybercrime and criminal laws have too often been used to target journalists. With elections approaching, authorities must not ignore the damaging impact of these charges on press freedom and journalists' ability to report freely and without fear." Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The charges are linked to four related investigations FIJ published between late 2023 and early 2024, which uncovered a number of suspicious government contracts by the office of the special assistant to the Nigerian government on sustainable development goals, Princess Adejoke Orelope-Adefulire.

Fear surrounding the Ebola outbreak, which has exploded into the second-worst on record since it was detected in May, has led to attacks on medical workers and raised the risk for reporters trying to counter rampant misinformation, with CPJ documenting attacks on two radio stations in the past week. On November 4, at least six unidentified individuals beat Jackson Mbusa Vagheni, editor-in-chief of Radio du Peuple Oïcha, a community radio station in the North Kivu province town of Oïcha, as he was leaving his office. The reports had emerged after an article in The Atlantic cited results from an AI detection tool, which suggested that the story may have been generated by artificial intelligence. Kundizeza won the 2026 Caine Prize for African Writing, which comes with a $13,000 endowment; however, the allegations prompted the Caine Prize to conduct an internal review, which included interviews with the author, judges, publishers, and independent expert analyses of the story's draft metadata. Following the investigation, the prize's board said it had found no evidence of generative AI use, and confirmed that Kundizeza remains the winner. The organization explained that the matter is now closed, while announcing the introduction of new measures to help guard against AI misuse in future submissions.

Le journaliste ivoiro-nigérien Serge Mathurin Adou a été condamné par la cour criminelle de Niamey à deux ans de prison ferme pour « atteinte à la défense nationale », le 21 novembre 2025. © Facebook Serge Mathurin Adou Par Jeune Afrique Publié aujourd'hui à 17h38 Lecture : 1 minute. Il avait disparu à Niamey le 1er septembre 2024 , après avoir indiqué à son épouse qu’il devait répondre à une convocation de la police. Quelques semaines plus tard, le ministre burkinabè de la Sécurité, Mahamadou Sana, pays allié du Niger , l’accusait d’être impliqué dans un « complot » et dans « plusieurs tentatives de déstabilisation » visant son pays. la suite après cette publicité « Il est rentré chez lui » Le journaliste avait ensuite été inculpé le 11 novembre 2024 pour « atteinte à la sûreté de l’État » et placé en détention préventive dans une prison en province, avant d’ être condamné à deux ans de prison en novembre 2025 . « Après avoir purgé ses deux ans de prison, Serge a été libéré ce matin [mercredi] à 9 heures et il est déjà rentré chez lui », a déclaré un responsable de la communauté ivoirienne à Niamey qui a requis l’anonymat. « Nous venons d’apprendre la libération ce mercredi matin de notre confrère Serge Mathurin », a indiqué un autre proche du journaliste, ce qu’a confirmé Canal 3, la chaîne de télévision privée nigérienne qui l’employait. la suite après cette publicité Serge Mathurin Adou, originaire de Côte d’Ivoire , vit au Niger depuis une vingtaine d’années.

stories.title: Ethiopia: Ethiopia Tells UN Envoy Eritrea, Sudan Backing Armed Groups and Drone Attacks
stories.summary: Ethiopia Tells UN Envoy Eritrea, Sudan Backing Armed Groups and Drone Attacks Sufian Abdul-Mouty/UNFPA Recently arriving refugees from Tigray (file photo). 11 November 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia has accused Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki and Sudan's army chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan of supporting, arming and coordinating armed groups operating inside Ethiopia, including through repeated drone attacks, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's Horn of Africa adviser Getachew K. Getachew disclosed the accusations following a meeting on Wednesday with Guang Cong, the UN Secretary-General's Special Envoy for the Horn of Africa, during which they discussed conflicts in Sudan and Somalia, as well as what he described as Eritrea's destabilizing role in the region. In a statement posted on his official social media account, Getachew said he had presented Ethiopia's position on what he described as activities by the Eritrean and Sudanese leadership to equip and coordinate armed elements inside Ethiopia. He also accused them of carrying out repeated drone attacks inside the country. Getachew said he had urged both governments to stop supporting and arming the groups, arguing that doing so was necessary for meaningful dialogue and to prevent further escalation.

stories.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PGDc Prefer DW on Google European colonialism was marked by the — often extremely violent — exploitation of people and resources. [Pictured: Clearing of land by setting grass on fire during a German research expedition to Tendaguru in German East Africa, 1909–1913] Image: Archiv/Museum für Naturkunde Advertisement Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men." But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust . Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history. 'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial history. [Pictured: Cans of Zyklon B gas, Auschwitz-Birkenau, German Nazi concentration and extermination camp in Poland] Image: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO "I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposed to be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case." "Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story. From colonial brutality to Nazi rule The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers.

stories.title: Kenyan Domestic Worker Sentenced to 100 Lashes in Saudi Arabia
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT A Saudi court has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage. stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Country by country, the Trump administration has been negotiating secretive agreements with nations across Africa to provide health aid under strict conditions. The agreements, structured to benefit the United States, are undermining efforts to prepare the world for the next pandemic, putting even Americans at risk, public health experts warn. In one striking example, under an agreement signed in February that was never made public, the United States is set to stop funding health care workers in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of the year. Congo has been struggling to contain an Ebola outbreak that has topped 10,000 cases and has spread to two other regions of Africa. The plan, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, provides Congo with $900 million over the next five years, and was signed before the Ebola outbreak was detected.

stories.title: 'Devastating message' as ANC records worst-ever result in South Africa election
stories.summary: Image source, EPA Image caption, Voters cast their ballots at a polling station during South Africa's local government elections in Johannesburg By Ed Habershon Reporting from Johannesburg Published 8 November 2026 South Africa's ANC has recorded its worst-ever showing in local elections since Nelson Mandela led the country out of apartheid and into democracy more than 30 years ago, a result the party has called "catastrophic". While it won the most votes of all parties in the country, the African National Congress won 31% of the overall vote, one third down from the 46% it gained in 2021, and a far cry from the 65% 20 years ago. The story of its decline is also clear in the provinces and cities. The party won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo. It also won the most votes in just two of the eight cities, compared with six at the last local elections.

stories.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
stories.summary: Daniel Oyegade on the shoot for Homage, a See My World production. Photograph: Omar Balaa View image in fullscreen Daniel Oyegade on the shoot for Homage, a See My World production. The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

stories.title: South Africa’s Politics May Never Be the Same Again
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Few things unite South Africans like a dry faucet. That’s what thousands of residents of Africa’s richest city, Johannesburg, woke up to on Wednesday before voting in local government elections. From the impoverished mostly Black township of Diepsloot to the racially mixed upper-middle-class Midrand to exclusive Hyde Park, which the president calls home, many voters expressed the same frustration as they left the polls. “Now, we don’t have water,” said Luleka Ngqangqashe, 35 and unemployed. “Imagine.” Some chalked up the Election Day outages to divine timing, others to political sabotage and still others to, well, life in Johannesburg. In any case, they were a reminder of the government failures that led the overwhelming majority of voters in this city of nearly five million people to vote against the nation’s once-dominant political, social and moral force: the African National Congress. With most of the votes tallied by Sunday, the A.N.C. was projected to win around 20 percent of the vote in Johannesburg, down from 33 percent in the last local election five years ago.

stories.title: Islamist Militant Attack Forces Patients to Flee Ebola Clinic in Congo
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Militants affiliated with the Islamic State burned down a health center treating Ebola patients in the Democratic Republic of Congo this week, forcing infected patients to flee amid violence that killed dozens of people, according to health and United Nations officials. At least 48 people were killed in the attacks, officials said. It started late Thursday with a series of attacks in and around Cantine-Aloya, a village about 28 miles west of Beni, a city in eastern Congo. Several dozen homes and shops were burned, forcing residents to flee the area. Two other health facilities were also set on fire.

stories.title: The young Somali woman changing how the world sees Mogadishu
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Somalia has the longest coastline in mainland Africa By Fardowsa Hanshi BBC Somali Published 7 November 2026 As the sun rises over the Indian Ocean, waves lap onto the golden sands while palm fronds rustle in the cool sea breeze. This is the image that one young Somali woman wants the world to have of her home city - in contrast to the one of suicide attacks and young men wielding AK-47s that many people currently associate with Somalia's capital. Sucdi Abdul Fattah Abdul Khader is among a growing number of local guides taking visitors beyond the headlines to explore Mogadishu's beauty spots, historic sites and culture. Her favourite spot is Jazeera beach, where visitors can enjoy the sea before heading to nearby sand dunes. "It's one of the tourist attractions where we bring our guests. It's a nice place," says the 23-year-old.

stories.title: Kenya Cult Leader Handed 200 Year Prison Sentence for Mass Murder
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT A Kenyan court on Friday sentenced a cult leader to 200 years in prison after he was convicted last month of murdering 190 children and an adult who were forced to starve themselves to death. The cult leader, Paul Nthenge Mackenzie, had ordered his followers to stop eating in order to meet Jesus, and aides had violently enforced the edict, a court in the Kenyan port city of Mombasa heard during the trial. Mackenzie received the longest sentence, 28 other people were also convicted for their roles in the massacre. Most of the children who died were under 10 years old. Mackenzie, a former taxi driver and small-time televangelist, was arrested in 2023 after the Kenyan authorities exhumed the bodies of more than 400 people who died in the preceding two years in the Shakahola Forest, a remote area of southeastern Kenya near the Indian Ocean.

stories.title: Tundu Lissu: After escaping the death penalty, what does his guilty verdict mean for Tanzania's democracy?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PHqy Prefer DW on Google Opposition figure Tundu Lissu originally faced the death penalty for treason Image: ChademaTZ2/X Advertisement On November 6, Tundu Lissu, leader of Tanzania 's main opposition Chadema party, was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections. The same day, he was cleared of treason charges — which could have meant a death sentence if he had been found guilty. Lissu commented that the judiciary had acted under pressure and rejected the verdict due to the fact that incitement was not among the charges brought against him at the start of his trial in 2025. Chadema officials have now signaled an intention to appeal the court decision. The government has not issued a statement on his conviction yet.

stories.title: Who’s Hiding Secrets About Dag Hammarskjöld’s Death?
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT For a long time, the 1961 plane crash that killed the U.N. secretary general Dag Hammarskjöld has been a mystery: a nighttime catastrophe in Cold War Africa, unexplained and unexplainable. In recent years, United Nations investigators have pushed for answers : What really happened to Mr. Hammarskjöld, a Swedish diplomatic titan who led the United Nations through Cold War rivalries and decolonization? Or an assassination ? “We deserve answers,” Caroline Hammarskjöld, the diplomat’s great-niece, said in an interview. “If it was an attack, then we have the right to know.” A much-anticipated report released by the United Nations this week said it provided no definitive answers because the lead investigator was “almost certain” that the United States, Britain and South Africa had not disclosed all their documents related to the case. The State Department said in a statement to The New York Times that the United States had “cooperated extensively with this investigation, including by sharing thousands of pages of declassified documents.” The British government declined to comment, and the South African government did not immediately respond.

stories.title: Lana Nusseibeh’s U.N. Bid Collides With U.A.E.’s Role in Sudan
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT The United Arab Emirates hired Colombian mercenaries to fight alongside a notorious Sudanese paramilitary group that has been accused of genocide, United Nations investigators have found. A confidential report submitted to the Security Council last week and obtained by The New York Times details how an Emirati security company with close ties to the government moved the Colombians into Sudan through territory controlled by Emirati proxies in Libya and Somalia. The report is the most detailed accounting yet by the United Nations of the Emirati role in Sudan’s civil war , in which the Emirates is accused of supplying drones, weapons and mercenaries to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, or R.S.F., fueling a conflict that has caused hundreds of thousands of deaths. The U.N. findings come at a sensitive time for the Emirates. One of its top diplomats, Lana Zaki Nusseibeh, who for years has led Emirati efforts to deny her country’s role in Sudan, is a candidate to become the next secretary general of the United Nations.
